title: Offline-first apps: why your app needs offline mode
description: Why Indian apps need offline mode: Google's offline-first rules, write strategies, sync and conflicts, PWA storage limits, examples and a developer checklist.

contentHtml:
What offline support means for an app

In short: Offline support means your app still opens, shows the last data it had and saves what the user does, even with no signal. Google's Android guide calls this an offline-first app: at a minimum it must read data without the network. For Indian users moving between good 4G, patchy rural coverage and lifts with no signal, it decides whether the app gets used or uninstalled.

This guide was checked in November 2026, against the official Android, MDN, web.dev and Firebase pages listed at the end, and the latest TRAI subscriber report.

In my experience, most business owners ask about offline mode after a complaint. A salesperson says the order screen spun for a minute inside a basement godown. A patient says the app showed a blank page on a train. The fix is not a better spinner. It is deciding, before the build, which parts of the app must work with no network and how the data catches up later.

I will go through what Google's own guidance says, how to pick a write strategy for each feature, three worked examples from Indian businesses, the mistakes I see most, and a checklist you can hand to whoever builds your app.

Why connectivity in India is uneven

India has a lot of internet users. It does not follow that every user has a good connection at every moment. TRAI's latest quarterly report shows the gap between urban and rural access.

Internet subscribers in India, quarter ending 30 June 2026

MeasureFigure
Total internet subscribers1,114.17 million
Wireless (fixed and mobile) internet subscribers1,066.43 million
Fixed (wired) internet subscribers47.73 million
Rural internet subscribers448.08 million
Urban internet subscribers per 100 people129.03
Rural internet subscribers per 100 people49.07

Source: TRAI quarterly performance indicators, via PIB and TRAI performance indicators reports page, read 16 November 2026.

Two things stand out. Almost all of those connections are wireless, so your users are on mobile data that comes and goes as they move. And rural access per 100 people is well under half of urban access. If your customers include farmers, rural retailers, field staff or anyone who travels for work, a large share of their sessions will happen on weak or no signal.

Subscriber counts do not measure signal quality, and I have not found an official source that publishes how often Indian users lose connection. So I will not give you a number for that. What Google's guidance does list is the everyday reality: limited bandwidth, short interruptions such as an elevator or a tunnel, and devices that are only online now and then, such as Wi-Fi-only tablets. Every one of those is common in Indian offices, shops and homes.

If you are building for users outside the metros, our post on building for Bharat covers language and device choices that sit alongside this.

What Google's offline-first guidance actually says

The clearest official definition is in Android's Build an offline-first app guide. An offline-first app "is able to perform all, or a critical subset of its core functionality without access to the internet." To work offline, the guide says the app must be able to do three things:

  • Remain usable without a reliable network connection.
  • Present users with local data immediately, instead of waiting for the first network call to complete or fail.
  • Fetch data in a way that is conscious of battery and data, for example only when charging or on Wi-Fi.

The key design rule follows from that. The data stored on the phone, which the guide calls the local data source, is the canonical source of truth for the app. Screens read only from it. The server, the network data source, is synchronised with the local copy in the background. The guide is explicit that the screens and business logic must never talk to the network directly.

This sounds like a technical detail. It is the decision that makes offline work possible. If every screen calls the server and waits, there is nothing to show when the call fails. If every screen reads a local database that a background job keeps fresh, the app opens instantly and still works in a basement.

Note what the guide does not demand. An app is offline-first if it can read without a network. Writing offline is optional and harder, because of conflicts, which I cover below. You can start with reads and add offline writes only where they matter.

Choose a write strategy for each feature

This is where most of the real decisions sit. Android's guide names three strategies for saving data. Each feature in your app should get one, chosen on purpose.

The three write strategies from Android's offline-first guide

StrategyWhat happensGoogle's guidance on when to use itIndian business example
Online-only writesSend to the server; if it fails, tell the userTransactions that must happen in near real time, such as a bank transferPaying an invoice, booking the last slot at a clinic
Queued writesPut the item in a queue and send it when back online, with retriesData that is not time sensitive and where failure need not be shown, such as analytics and logsApp usage events, crash logs
Lazy writesSave on the phone first, then send at the earliest chanceData that is critical, where losing it is unacceptableA field order, a delivery photo, a visit note

Source: Android Developers, Build an offline-first app, read 16 November 2026.

For online-only writes, the guide suggests not showing the write option at all when offline, or disabling it, and telling the user with a message they can see. That is better than letting someone fill a long form and then fail.

Lazy writes are what most business owners mean when they say offline mode. The salesperson taps save, the order is stored on the phone, and the app sends it when the signal returns. Google's own example is a to-do app where tasks added offline must be stored locally to avoid losing data.

Syncing and conflicts, in plain words

Once data is saved on the phone, it has to reach the server. Android's guide describes two ways of keeping the two in step.

Pull-based sync fetches fresh data when the user opens a screen. It is easier to build and never fetches data nobody looks at. The guide warns it can use a lot of data if screens refetch unchanged information, and it works best when offline periods are short.

Push-based sync downloads a baseline on first start, then waits for the server to say something has changed and fetches only that. The guide says such an app can stay offline indefinitely and uses minimum data, but versioning data for conflict resolution is not trivial and the server has to support it. Many apps mix the two: pull for a busy feed, push for the user's own profile.

A conflict happens when two people, or one person on two devices, change the same record while offline. The guide says resolving conflicts usually needs versioning, and that for mobile apps a common approach is "last write wins": each device stamps its change with a time, and the server keeps the newest.

Last write wins is fine for a profile picture. It is risky for stock counts or money, where two changes should add up rather than one replacing the other. That is a business decision, not a coding one, so the owner should make it. Ask your developer which records can conflict, and what the rule is for each.

On Android, the guide recommends WorkManager for the queues and retries. WorkManager lets tasks persist across app restarts and device reboots, and its constraints can hold work until the device is on an unmetered network, idle or has enough battery. For retries, the guide suggests exponential backoff, waiting longer between each attempt, and not retrying requests that failed because the user is not authorised.

Offline for web apps and PWAs

If your product is a website or a progressive web app rather than a native app, the tools are different but the idea is the same.

MDN's service worker guide explains that a service worker lets a site use cached assets first, giving a default experience offline before fetching more from the network. Service workers only run over HTTPS, with localhost allowed for development. The web.dev Offline Cookbook lists the common patterns, including caching the app shell on install, serving from cache and falling back to the network, and stale-while-revalidate, which shows the cached copy and refreshes it in the background.

Browser storage has limits you should know before you promise offline mode on the web. MDN's page on storage quotas and eviction says data is stored as best-effort by default, which means the browser may delete it under storage pressure. In Chromium browsers such as Chrome and Edge an origin can use up to 60% of total disk. Safari also proactively deletes script-created data for sites with no user interaction in the last seven days of browser use, when cross-site tracking prevention is on. You can ask for persistent storage with navigator.storage.persist(), which the browser may grant or refuse.

The Background Synchronization API, which would let a web app send queued data after the tab is closed, is marked by MDN as limited availability and not Baseline, because it does not work in some widely used browsers. So on the web, plan for queued data to go out the next time the user opens the site.

Build it yourself or use a managed sync service

Android's guide describes two routes. A custom stack uses a local database such as Room, your own network client and WorkManager jobs, and gives you full control over conflict rules. A managed service such as Cloud Firestore handles the disk cache, offline write queue and sync for you.

If you go the managed route, read the defaults. Firebase's offline data page says offline persistence is on by default for Android and Apple platforms but off by default for the web, and that on the web it is supported only in Chrome, Safari and Firefox. The default cache threshold is 100 MB. Firebase also warns that the web cache is not cleared between sessions, so an app handling sensitive information should ask whether the user is on a trusted device before turning persistence on.

Neither route is right for everyone. A managed service is quicker to ship. A custom stack is easier to bend when your conflict rules are unusual, such as stock that two people edit at once.

Step by step: plan offline support before the build

This is the order I would follow with any business app.

Step 1. List the jobs users do away from good signal. Walk through a real day. Where does your salesperson, delivery rider or patient use the app? A godown, a lift, a village, a hospital corridor. Write down the screens they need there.

Step 2. Mark each screen read-only or read-write offline. Many screens only need to show the last known data: a price list, a patient's past visits, today's route. Those are the easy wins.

Step 3. Give every save action a write strategy. Online-only, queued or lazy, using the table above. Anything involving money or a limited slot usually stays online-only.

Step 4. Decide the conflict rule for shared records. For each record that two people can change, decide: newest wins, or changes are combined, or a person reviews it. Put it in writing.

Step 5. Design the offline states. The user should always know three things: this is saved on the phone, this has reached the server, this failed and needs action. A small sync status on each item beats a full-screen error.

Step 6. Set what is downloaded and when. Decide how much data the app keeps on the phone and when it refreshes, keeping Google's advice about battery and data in mind. A rider does not need last year's deliveries.

Step 7. Test with the network actually off. Airplane mode, a weak signal, the app killed halfway through a sync, the phone restarted with items in the queue. Each should end with no lost data.

If you want this written down with a fixed price before any build starts, that is what our ₹3,500 requirement analysis covers: a call with the people who would build it, the requirements worked through, and a written fixed quotation and timeline (book it here). Code, cloud and credentials stay in your name.

Three worked examples from Indian businesses

These are illustrative. The businesses and numbers are made up to show the decisions, not taken from real clients.

A distributor's field sales app

An FMCG distributor in Telangana has, say, 30 salespeople visiting kirana shops. Many shops are in market lanes or villages where the signal drops.

The product catalogue, prices and each shop's outstanding balance should be readable offline, downloaded every morning on Wi-Fi at the office or at the start of the route. New orders are lazy writes: saved on the phone first with a clear "waiting to send" mark, then sent when the signal returns. Stock availability is the hard part. If two salespeople sell the last 20 cartons offline, last write wins would quietly lose one order. The owner should decide that orders are always accepted and stock shortfalls are handled at the godown, and tell the developer.

A home healthcare or clinic app

A clinic chain sends nurses for home visits. The nurse needs the patient's address, history and today's tasks, sometimes in buildings with poor coverage.

The visit list and patient summary are read offline. Visit notes and vital signs are lazy writes, because losing them is not acceptable. Booking a new appointment slot stays online-only, because two people could take the same slot. Because this is health data, the cached data on the phone needs the same care as data on the server: encrypted storage, sign-out that clears it, and only the records the nurse needs that day.

A logistics proof-of-delivery app

A delivery company's riders capture a photo and the receiver's name at the door. Some apartment basements have no signal at all.

The day's route and parcel list are downloaded at the hub. The delivery confirmation and photo are lazy writes with WorkManager retrying in the background, ideally waiting for a connection before uploading heavy photos. The customer-facing tracking page should say "delivered, awaiting sync" rather than showing the parcel as still out for delivery. For more on this kind of system, see our page on logistics apps.

Common mistakes that break offline mode

Treating offline as a later feature. If screens call the server directly, adding offline later means rewriting the data layer. Google's guidance puts the local data source at the centre from the start for a reason.

Showing a spinner forever. A request with no timeout and no cached data is the worst of both. Show what you have, and say when it was last updated.

Silently losing saved data. A queue held only in memory dies when Android kills the app. Queued and lazy writes should be stored on disk and handled by persistent work.

Using last write wins everywhere. It is the common default. It is wrong for counts, balances and anything where two changes should combine.

Promising offline on the web without reading the limits. Best-effort storage can be evicted, Safari has its seven-day rule, and Background Sync is not available in every browser.

Downloading everything. Keeping a full year of data on a budget phone wastes storage and data. Sync what the user needs for the job. Our post on designing for low-end devices goes into storage and memory limits.

Testing only on office Wi-Fi. Offline bugs show up on a moving train, not at a desk.

A checklist to give your developer

  • Which screens read from local data, and how fresh that data is shown to be.
  • For every save action: online-only, queued or lazy.
  • Where the offline queue is stored, and what happens after the app is killed or the phone restarts.
  • The retry rule: backoff, maximum attempts, and which errors are not retried.
  • The conflict rule for every record two people can change.
  • What the user sees for saved, synced and failed items.
  • How much data is kept on the phone, and when it refreshes (Wi-Fi only, charging, or any network).
  • For web apps: service worker caching strategy, storage persistence request, and what happens in Safari.
  • How cached personal data is protected and cleared on sign-out.
  • A test plan that includes airplane mode, weak signal and restarts mid-sync.

If you are planning an Android, iOS or cross-platform app, our mobile app development page explains how we scope builds like this.

Frequently asked questions

What is an offline-first app?

Android's guide defines it as an app that can perform all, or a critical subset, of its core functionality without internet access. At a minimum it must be able to read data without the network. The data on the phone is the source of truth, and the server is synchronised in the background.

Does every app need offline mode?

No. An app that only makes payments or live bookings can stay online-only, as long as it tells users clearly when they are offline. Most business apps benefit from at least offline reading of recent data, because mobile signal in India is uneven.

Is offline support expensive to add?

It is cheaper to plan from the start than to add later, because it shapes how the app stores and reads data. I have not found reliable published figures on the extra cost, so ask for it as a separate line in your quotation.

How does an app handle two people editing the same record offline?

That is a conflict. Android's guide says conflict resolution usually needs versioning, and that last write wins is a common approach for mobile apps. For stock, balances or anything that should add up, decide a different rule and write it into the requirements.

Can a website or PWA work offline?

Yes, with a service worker, which needs HTTPS. Browser storage is best-effort by default and can be evicted, Safari may delete script data for sites not used in seven days, and the Background Sync API is not available in every browser.

Does Firebase work offline?

Cloud Firestore's offline persistence is on by default for Android and Apple apps and off by default on the web, where it is supported only in Chrome, Safari and Firefox. The default cache threshold is 100 MB.

How should offline mode be tested?

Turn on airplane mode, use a weak signal, kill the app during a sync and restart the phone with items still queued. Every case should end with the data on the server and nothing lost or duplicated.
